explain.title: Spreadsheets
explain.body: Spreadsheets are tools that help us organise data in rows and columns, much like a simpler version of a database. They are often used for tasks that don't require complex data management. Spreadsheets like Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets allow users to input data into cells organised in rows and columns. You can perform calculations, create charts, and sort data easily. These are commonly used for personal budgeting, simple data analysis, and small business inventory management.

explain.title: Databases
explain.body: Databases are like digital filing cabinets where information is stored in an organised way. They are designed to handle large amounts of structured data and allow users to easily find and manipulate this data. Information in databases is stored in tables, similar to spreadsheets. Each table has rows and columns, where rows represent individual records, and columns represent the attributes of those records. These are used in many everyday applications like banking systems, online shopping websites, and school records.

explain.title: Data warehouses
explain.body: Data Warehouses are specialized types of databases designed for storing and analysing large amounts of data collected from various sources. They are used to help organizations make decisions based on data analysis. Data warehouses are used by companies to analyze business performance, track sales, and understand customer behaviour. Examples include Amazon Redshift and Google BigQuery.

explain.title: NoSQL
explain.body: NoSQL stands for "Not Only SQL" and refers to a variety of database technologies that are designed to handle different types of data that may not fit well into traditional databases. NoSQL databases are flexible and can store unstructured data, which is data that doesn't follow a specific format. Unlike traditional databases that use tables, NoSQL databases can use various structures like documents, key-value pairs, graphs, or columns to store data. NoSQL databases are often used in big data applications, real-time web applications, and content management systems.

mistakes: Do not confuse a spreadsheet with a database: both can use rows and columns, but spreadsheets suit simpler tasks and databases are designed to handle large amounts of structured data.
Do not say that data warehouses are just for storing everyday records; they are designed for storing and analysing large amounts of data from various sources.
Do not describe NoSQL as meaning "no data" or as only one format; it stands for "Not Only SQL" and can use several structures.
In a database table, do not reverse the terms: rows represent records and columns represent attributes.
When choosing a storage method, do not give only its name; connect it to the task it is suited for.

explain.title: Pre-processing prepares the data
explain.body: Data pre-processing is the first and most important step in working with data. It involves getting the data ready for analysis by cleaning and organizing it. Before analysis, check that data is accurate, complete, reliable, consistent, and up-to-date.

explain.title: Find and deal with data problems
explain.body: Errors are mistakes in the data. Outliers are unusual or extreme values that don't fit the pattern of the rest of the data. Biases are distortions that affect the accuracy of the data. Validation checks completeness and accuracy; cleaning corrects or removes errors and decides how to handle missing values and outliers.

explain.title: Quantitative analysis uses numbers
explain.body: Quantitative analysis deals with numbers and measurable data. The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value when the values are arranged in order; with an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the value that appears most frequently.

explain.title: Measures of spread describe variation
explain.body: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values. Variance measures how spread out the values are from the mean, using S² = ∑(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1). Standard deviation is the square root of the variance, using S = √[∑(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)].

explain.title: Qualitative analysis studies non-numeric data
explain.body: Qualitative analysis deals with non-numeric data such as text, images, and sounds. Content analysis counts how often specific words or themes appear. Thematic analysis identifies and interprets themes or patterns within the data.

mistakes: Calling any unusual value an error: an outlier may be an unusual but true value, so investigate it before changing or removing it.

Using the mean when an extreme value strongly distorts it; the median can give a better typical value in that situation.
Forgetting to arrange data in order before finding the median.
Using n instead of n − 1 in the sample variance or standard deviation formula shown in your textbook.
Mixing up content analysis and thematic analysis: content analysis counts appearances, while thematic analysis identifies and interprets patterns.

notes.answer: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.
notes.explanation: Data is raw facts collected about things around us. It can be processed to make useful information. Data may be numbers, words, measurements, observations, images, or sounds, and can come from different sources.
notes.simple: Data is unprocessed information we collect. When we work with it, it can help us understand something or make a decision.
examples: Weather data includes temperature, humidity, and wind speed collected from weather stations.
A store may record the number of products sold and their prices.
steps: Collect facts about something.
Process those facts.
Use them to produce useful information.
notes.checkAnswer: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.

notes.title: Choosing the right data type
notes.answer: Qualitative data is descriptive or categorical; quantitative data is numerical. Nominal categories have no order, ordinal categories have a meaningful order, discrete data is countable, and continuous data can take any value within a range.
notes.explanation: Data types describe what kind of information we have. Qualitative data uses descriptions or categories; quantitative data uses numbers. Qualitative data may be nominal or ordinal, while quantitative data may be discrete or continuous.
notes.simple: Ask what the data tells you: a label or description is qualitative; a measured or counted number is quantitative. Then check whether categories have an order or whether numbers are counted or measured.
examples: A student's favourite fruit is qualitative, nominal data: it is a category with no implied order.
A student's height is quantitative, continuous data: it is measured and can include decimals.
steps: If the information is a label or category, it is qualitative.
If qualitative categories have no order, they are nominal; if they have a meaningful order, they are ordinal.
If the information is a number, it is quantitative.
If a number counts separate items, it is discrete; if it measures a value that can include fractions or decimals, it is continuous.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of data is the number of students in a class, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: The number of students is discrete data because it is counted in separate whole numbers.

notes.title: Organising and Analysing Data
notes.answer: Organised data is easier to find, understand, compare and analyse.
notes.explanation: Organising data makes it clearer, quicker to use and easier to analyse. Data can be collected using methods such as surveys, questionnaires, interviews and observations, then organised into tables, charts or graphs. Information from online sources can be extracted and integrated to build a fuller understanding of a topic.
notes.simple: Put information in a neat, useful form so it is easier to understand and compare.
examples: A table of students' marks makes it easier to compare their scores in different subjects.
For a project on social media, you could collect information from several websites, save relevant statistics and combine similar findings.
steps: Collect information using a suitable method, such as a survey or observation.
Arrange the information neatly in a table, chart or graph.
Look for patterns, trends or similarities.
Combine useful information from different sources when a fuller picture is needed.
notes.checkQuestion: Why can organising data into tables or charts help when analysing it?
notes.checkAnswer: Organising data into tables, charts and graphs makes it clearer and easier to find, compare and analyse.

notes.title: Structured and Unstructured Data
notes.answer: Structured data is organised in a format that is easy to search and analyse; unstructured data is free-form and does not fit a specific format.
notes.explanation: Structured data is organised and formatted to be easily searchable and analysable. Unstructured data is more free-form and doesn't fit into a specific format. Structured data is often stored in rows and columns, while unstructured data includes items such as emails, social media posts, videos, and images.
notes.simple: Structured data is neatly arranged. Unstructured data is not arranged in a fixed format.
examples: A student spreadsheet with columns for Student ID, Name, Class, and Fee Status is structured data.
An email or a video is unstructured data.
steps: Look for a fixed arrangement, such as rows and columns.
If the data is arranged in a searchable format, identify it as structured data.
If it is free-form and does not fit a specific format, identify it as unstructured data.
notes.checkQuestion: Is a spreadsheet of student records structured or unstructured data, and why?
notes.checkAnswer: A student spreadsheet is structured data because it is organised in rows and columns. A video is unstructured data because it does not fit into that format.

notes.title: Choosing a way to store data
notes.answer: The four technologies are spreadsheets, databases, data warehouses, and NoSQL.
notes.explanation: Data storage techniques are ways to save and organise information so it can be accessed and used later. Spreadsheets arrange data in rows and columns; databases store structured data in tables; data warehouses store and analyse large amounts of data from different sources; NoSQL databases can store flexible, unstructured data.
notes.simple: Choose a storage method that suits the data and the job. A spreadsheet suits simpler tasks; a database suits structured records; a data warehouse suits large-scale analysis; NoSQL suits flexible data that does not fit traditional tables.
examples: A small shop could use a spreadsheet to keep a simple inventory.
A company could use a data warehouse to analyse sales collected from different sources.
steps: Check whether the task is simple or needs complex data management.
Check whether the data is structured in tables or is flexible and unstructured.
Choose the method that fits the task: spreadsheet, database, data warehouse, or NoSQL.
notes.checkQuestion: Name the four data storage technologies covered in this section.
notes.checkAnswer: Spreadsheets, databases, data warehouses, and NoSQL.

notes.title: Data Visualization

notes.simple: A chart is a picture of data. It can make a lot of information easier to understand quickly.

A line graph can show how a measurement changes over time.

Choose a suitable chart or graph for that data type.

notes.title: Preparing and Analysing Data
notes.explanation: Data pre-processing gets data ready for analysis by checking its quality, finding problems, and cleaning or organizing it. Analysis then uses suitable methods to find useful information. Numerical data can be studied using measures such as the mean, median, mode, range, variance, and standard deviation. Non-numeric data can be studied using content analysis or thematic analysis.
notes.simple: First check and tidy the data. Then choose a suitable way to study it: use number methods for numeric data and look for words or themes in non-numeric data.
examples: If a score is recorded as 105 when the maximum is 100, it is an error that should be checked and corrected or removed.
For the scores 70, 80, 90, 100, and 110, the mean is 90.
steps: Check whether the data is accurate, complete, reliable, consistent, and up-to-date.
Identify errors, outliers, and possible biases.
Validate completeness and accuracy, then clean the data as needed.
Use quantitative methods for numbers and qualitative methods for non-numeric data.
Interpret the results to discover useful information and draw conclusions.

notes.title: Cloud Storage and Working Together
notes.answer: A backup can help you recover a file if it is accidentally deleted or your computer fails.
notes.explanation: Cloud storage lets you save files online and access them from different devices. Remote access means using a computer, network, or its resources from a distant location. Backups are separate copies that help you recover files if the originals are lost. Collaborative authoring lets several people work on the same document or project together.
notes.simple: Think of cloud storage as an online place for your files. You can reach your files from another device, keep backup copies, and work with other people on shared documents.
examples: Save a school project to Google Drive at home, then open and edit it at school.
Keep a copy of a computer file on Google Drive or a USB so you can recover it if the computer crashes.
steps: Save your file online or make a separate backup copy.
Log in to your cloud account from the device you want to use.
Open the file and continue working.
For a shared project, let group members contribute and edit.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one reason to make a backup of an important file?
notes.checkAnswer: Remote access lets you connect to and use a computer or network from a distant location.

notes.title: How data science turns data into insights
notes.answer: Data science combines computer skills, math, and business knowledge to turn raw data into useful insights.
notes.explanation: Data science uses data to understand problems and make better decisions. It brings together computer science, mathematics and statistics, and business knowledge. A data science workflow moves from identifying a problem to collecting, cleaning, analysing, interpreting, and visualizing data.
notes.simple: Data science is detective work with data: find information, check it, look for clues, understand what they mean, and show the results clearly.
examples: A school collects students’ arrival times, checks the data for errors, looks for patterns, works out likely reasons for lateness, and presents the results in a chart.
A sports team analyses performance data to find patterns and develop better strategies.
steps: Identify and clearly define the problem.
Collect information from suitable sources.
Clean the data by fixing errors and organizing it.
Analyse the data to look for patterns or answers.
Interpret the results and draw conclusions.
Visualize the data with charts or graphs to make it easier to understand.

notes.title: Big Data and its applications
notes.answer: Big Data is extremely large and complex data that cannot be managed with traditional tools. Its Three Vs are Volume, Velocity, and Variety.
notes.explanation: Big Data is extremely large and complex data that traditional tools cannot manage easily. Its Three Vs describe how much data there is, how quickly it moves, and the different forms it takes.
notes.simple: Think of Big Data as a huge, fast-moving collection of many kinds of information. Special tools help people find useful patterns in it.
examples: Social media posts, likes, and comments shared every day show Big Data's Volume.
A bank analysing transactions to spot unusual activity is an example of a Big Data application.

rationales: Correct: thematic analysis identifies and interprets themes or patterns in qualitative data.

Data validation checks completeness and accuracy, not common ideas in essays.
The mean is a numerical average and does not interpret essay themes.

quiz.stem: For the data set [2, 4, 6], what are the mean and sample variance?
options: The mean is 4 and the sample variance is 4
The mean is 4 and the sample variance is 2
The mean is 12 and the sample variance is 4
The mean is 4 and the sample variance is 8
rationales: Correct: the mean is 4 and the squared deviations sum to 8, so the sample variance is 8 ÷ (3 − 1) = 4.
The sample variance is 4, not 2; the denominator is n − 1, which is 2.
The mean is (2 + 4 + 6) ÷ 3 = 4, not 12.
The sum of squared deviations is 8, but it must be divided by n − 1, giving a variance of 4.

quiz.stem: What is a key use of cloud storage?
options: Save files online so they can be accessed from different devices
Make a computer work without electricity
Prevent anyone from editing a document
Store files only on one physical computer
rationales: This is correct: cloud storage saves files online so they can be accessed from different devices.
Cloud storage does not make a computer work without electricity.
Cloud storage can support sharing and collaborative editing rather than preventing all edits.
Cloud storage keeps files online, not only on one physical computer.

quiz.stem: What does remote access mean?
options: Using a nearby computer without an internet connection
Connecting to and using a computer or network from a distant location
Making a printed copy of a file
rationales: This describes local use without a connection, not access from a distant location.
This is correct: remote access means connecting to and using a computer or network from a distant location.
Printing a file does not mean connecting to a distant computer or network.
Deleting files is not the meaning of remote access.

quiz.stem: Which choice best describes a data backup?
options: A copy of important data stored separately from the original
A list of people who edited a file
A way to make a file larger
A document that cannot be changed
rationales: This is correct: a backup is a separate copy that can help protect against data loss.
A list of editors may help track changes, but it is not a backup copy.
Making a file larger does not protect it against data loss.
A file that cannot be changed is not necessarily a separate backup.

quiz.stem: What is collaborative authoring?
options: One person reads a printed document aloud
Several people work together to create and edit a document or project
A computer automatically deletes old files
A file is saved only on a USB
rationales: Reading aloud is not the process of jointly creating and editing a document.
This is correct: collaborative authoring involves multiple people creating, editing, and improving work together.
Deleting old files is not collaborative authoring.
Saving a file on a USB does not involve people working together on it.

quiz.stem: How can collaborative tools enhance productivity?
options: It can help students finish a project faster by working on different sections at the same time
It ensures that only one student can contribute
It removes the need to save files
It prevents group members from sharing ideas
rationales: This is correct: people can work on different sections simultaneously and complete the project faster.
Collaborative tools allow multiple people to contribute, not just one.
Working together does not remove the need to save files.
Collaborative tools can support sharing ideas rather than preventing it.

quiz.stem: What is one benefit of version control in a collaborative document?
options: It lets users return to previous versions and see who made changes
It makes every file available to everyone without permission
It stops a document from being edited
It changes a document into a printed book
rationales: This is correct: version control can show earlier versions and who made changes.
Version control does not mean every file is available to everyone without permission.
Version control does not prevent a document from being edited.
Version control does not turn a document into a printed book.

quiz.stem: Which action best protects a school project if a computer crashes?
options: Save a backup copy to a cloud service or USB
Close the file and delete the original
Leave the only copy on the computer
rationales: This is correct: a separate copy on a cloud service or USB can be recovered if the computer fails.
Deleting the original without a backup increases the chance of losing the work.
Renaming a file does not create a separate copy or protect it from computer failure.
Leaving the only copy on the computer does not protect it if that computer crashes.

quiz.stem: A student saved a project in Google Drive at home. What should the student do to work on it at school?
options: Log in to the cloud account from another device and open the project
Wait until the original computer is available
Create a new project and discard the saved one
Print the project and use only the paper copy
rationales: This is correct: logging in from another device lets the student access and continue working on the saved project.
Remote access means the student need not wait to use the original computer.
The saved project can be opened, so starting over and discarding it is unnecessary.
A paper copy does not allow the student to edit the saved online project.

quiz.stem: What is a main purpose of data science?
options: To turn raw data into useful insights
To make data harder to understand
To replace all decisions with guesses
To collect information without a problem to solve
rationales: Correct: data science uses data to find useful insights and support decisions.
Incorrect: data visualization and analysis aim to make findings easier to understand.
Incorrect: data science helps people make better-informed decisions, not guesses.
Incorrect: data collection is guided by a problem or question to investigate.

quiz.stem: Which fields are used to analyse data and find patterns?
rationales: Correct: mathematics and statistics help analyse data and identify patterns.
Incorrect: these are not the fields named in the section as supporting data analysis.
Incorrect: these are not the fields named in the section as supporting data analysis.
Incorrect: these are not the fields named in the section as supporting data analysis.

quiz.stem: Which step begins the data science workflow?
rationales: Incorrect: analysis happens after the problem is defined and data is collected and cleaned.
Correct: the workflow begins by understanding and clearly defining the problem.
Incorrect: visualization is used later to communicate results.
Incorrect: cleaning follows data collection, not problem identification.

quiz.stem: What does data cleaning involve?
options: Removing errors and organizing the collected data
Making a chart before gathering any information
rationales: Correct: data cleaning fixes mistakes and organizes data so it can be used.
Incorrect: a chart is a form of visualization, and this option places it before collecting data.
Incorrect: deciding what results mean is data interpretation.
Incorrect: choosing and defining the problem is problem identification.

quiz.stem: Which action is data interpretation?
options: Explaining what the analysed results mean
rationales: Incorrect: looking for patterns or answers is data analysis.
Correct: interpretation means understanding analysed results and drawing conclusions.
Incorrect: gathering information is data collection.
Incorrect: correcting errors is data cleaning.

quiz.stem: Why is data visualization useful?
options: It makes data easier to understand using charts and graphs
It replaces the need to collect data
It guarantees that every conclusion is correct
It removes the need to define a problem
rationales: Correct: charts and graphs can present data in a way that is easier to understand.
Incorrect: visualization presents data; it does not replace data collection.
Incorrect: a chart cannot guarantee that the analysis or conclusion is correct.
Incorrect: the workflow still begins by clearly defining the problem.

quiz.stem: Which field helps with handling and organizing data?
rationales: Correct: computer science helps with handling and organizing data.
Incorrect: business knowledge helps apply insights to real-life problems and decisions.
Incorrect: mathematics and statistics help analyse data and find patterns.
Incorrect: visualization is a workflow step, not one of the three fields listed.

quiz.stem: A student makes a bar chart to show which sports are most popular. Which workflow step is this?
rationales: Incorrect: collection is gathering the information, such as by conducting a survey.
Incorrect: interpretation is understanding the results and drawing conclusions.
Incorrect: cleaning is fixing errors and organizing the collected information.
Correct: making a chart to communicate data is data visualization.

quiz.stem: Which characteristic of Big Data describes the sheer amount of information collected?
options: The sheer amount of data collected
The speed at which data is generated and processed
The different forms data can take
rationales: Correct: Volume means the sheer amount of data collected.
Incorrect: Speed of generation and processing is Velocity.
Incorrect: Different forms of data are described by Variety.
Incorrect: Accuracy is not one of the Three Vs given in this section.

quiz.stem: A stream of posts is generated and processed very quickly; which Big Data characteristic does this show?
rationales: Incorrect: Volume concerns the amount of data, not how quickly it moves.
Correct: Velocity describes the speed at which data is generated and processed.
Incorrect: Variety concerns the different forms data can take.
Incorrect: Validation is not one of the Three Vs described here.

quiz.stem: Which example best demonstrates Variety in Big Data?
options: A company's customer reviews, product photos, and sales figures
A large number of identical temperature readings
A single database containing only numbers
rationales: Correct: It includes different data forms: text, images, and numbers.
Incorrect: Many readings may show Volume, but this example does not show different data forms.
Incorrect: This example contains only one form of data.
Incorrect: A fast connection is not an example of varied data.

quiz.stem: What is the purpose of predictive modelling?
options: Predict future events using historical data
rationales: Correct: Predictive modelling forecasts future events based on historical data.
Incorrect: Predictive modelling is not a method for storing photographs.
Incorrect: Alphabetical arrangement is not the purpose of predictive modelling.
Incorrect: Deleting old records is not what predictive modelling means.

quiz.stem: How can a transportation company use Big Data, according to this section?
options: Find the quickest routes and predict where rides will be needed
rationales: Correct: Transportation companies analyse past trips to optimise routes and predict ride demand.
Incorrect: Medical records are associated with healthcare rather than this transportation example.
Incorrect: Measuring taste is not the transportation application described.
Incorrect: Encryption is a privacy measure, not the route-management use described.

quiz.stem: Which task is a Big Data application in finance?
options: Detect unusual transactions that might indicate fraud
Recommend books based on a student's grades
Predict the weather using patient records
Create graphs of social media friendships
rationales: Correct: Banks analyse transactions to spot unusual activities that might indicate fraud.
Incorrect: Book recommendations are not the finance example in this section.
Incorrect: Patient records are used in healthcare, not for the described weather prediction.
Incorrect: Social-network connections are an example of graph analytics, not the finance application.

quiz.stem: Which tool is used to manage and query databases?
rationales: Correct: SQL is used to manage and query databases.
Incorrect: Matplotlib is used for creating graphs.
Incorrect: Excel is a spreadsheet program used to organise and analyse data.
Incorrect: Pandas is a Python library used for data manipulation.

quiz.stem: What future visualization advancement is described in this section?
options: Interactive dashboards that let users explore data from different angles
Tools that prevent users from viewing any charts
Removing all data from different regions
rationales: Correct: The section describes interactive dashboards for exploring data from different angles.
Incorrect: The section describes making data easier to explore, not hiding charts.
Incorrect: Increased automation is expected to reduce repetitive manual work.
Incorrect: Removing regional data is not described as a future visualization advancement.

quiz.stem:
Q9.1. What is data?
(a) Processed information (b) Raw facts gathered about things (c) A collection of numbers only (d) A list of observed events
rationales: This is not the definition of data; processed information is information produced from data.
This is correct: data are raw facts gathered about things.
Data are not limited to numbers; they can also be words, categories, or observations.
Observed events can provide data, but this is not the general definition.

quiz.stem:
Q9.2. Which of the following is an example of qualitative data?
(a) Temperature readings in degrees Celsius (b) Number of students in a class (c) Favourite ice cream flavours (d) Test scores out of 100
options: Number of students in a class
rationales: Temperature readings are numerical measurements, so they are quantitative.
A number of students is a count, so it is quantitative discrete data.
This is correct: flavour names describe categories, not numerical amounts.
Test scores are numerical, so they are quantitative.

quiz.stem:
Q9.3. What type of data involves distinct, separate values that are countable?
(a) Nominal Data (b) Ordinal Data (c) Discrete Data (d) Continuous Data
rationales: Nominal data name categories without an order; they are not defined as countable numerical values.
Ordinal data are categories with an order, not distinct countable numerical values.
This is correct: discrete data consist of distinct, separate, countable values.
Continuous data can take measured values throughout a range, rather than only separate countable values.

quiz.stem:
Q9.4. What is an example of continuous data?
(a) Number of cars in a parking lot (b) Height of students in centimetres (c) Types of fruits (d) Shirt sizes (small, medium, large)
options: Number of cars in a parking lot
rationales: Cars are counted in separate whole-number amounts, so this is discrete data.
This is correct: height is measured and can take values within a range.
Fruit types are categories, not continuous measurements.
These are ordered categories, not continuous measurements.

quiz.stem:
Q9.5. What type of data is used to categorize items without implying any order?
(a) Ordinal Data (b) Discrete Data (c) Nominal Data (d) Continuous Data
rationales: Ordinal data have categories that can be placed in an order.
Discrete data are countable numerical values, not unordered categories.
This is correct: nominal data categorize items without implying any order.
Continuous data are measurements that can take values within a range.

quiz.stem:
Q9.6. How can you organise data to make it easier to analyse?
(a) By writing it in long paragraphs (b) By creating tables, charts, and graphs (c) By storing it in random files (d) By keeping it in a messy notebook
options: By writing it in long paragraphs
By creating tables, charts, and graphs
By storing it in random files
By keeping it in a messy notebook
rationales: Long paragraphs make comparisons and patterns harder to find.
This is correct: tables, charts, and graphs organise data for easier analysis.
Random files make data difficult to find and compare.
A messy notebook does not organise information for analysis.

quiz.stem:
Q9.7. Which tool can be used to create surveys online?
(a) Microsoft Word (b) Google Forms
(c) Excel Spreadsheets (d) Adobe Photoshop
rationales: Word is mainly used for creating documents, not online surveys.
This is correct: Google Forms can be used to create online surveys.
Spreadsheets can organise data, but are not the survey-creation tool identified here.
Photoshop is an image-editing tool, not an online survey tool.

quiz.stem:
Q9.8. What is the main purpose of data collection?
(a) To create random numbers
(b) To gather information to answer questions or make decisions
(c) To delete old data
(d) To format text documents
options: To gather information to answer questions or make decisions
rationales: Creating random numbers is not the main purpose of data collection.
This is correct: data are gathered to answer questions or support decisions.
Deleting old data is not the purpose of collecting data.
Formatting documents is unrelated to the main purpose of data collection.

quiz.stem:
Q9.9. What is the primary purpose of data visualization?
(a) To generate random numbers (b) To convert text into data
(c) To make data easier to understand by turning it into pictures
(d) To hide complex data
options: To make data easier to understand by turning it into pictures
rationales: Generating random numbers is not data visualization.
Visualization displays data; it does not convert text into data.
This is correct: visualizations use pictures such as charts and graphs to make data easier to understand.
Visualization is used to clarify data, not hide it.

quiz.stem:
Q9.10. Which tool is specifically designed for creating detailed and interactive visualizations?
(a) Microsoft Excel (b) Google Sheets
(c) Tableau (d) PowerPoint
rationales: Excel can create charts, but it is not the tool identified as specifically designed for detailed, interactive visualizations.
Google Sheets can make charts, but it is not the tool identified here for detailed, interactive visualizations.
This is correct: Tableau is specifically designed for detailed and interactive visualizations.
PowerPoint is presentation software, rather than the tool identified for interactive visualizations.

quiz.stem:
Q9.11. What is the first step in the data science process?
(a) Data Cleaning (b) Data Analysis
(c) Data Collection (d) Understanding the problem
rationales: Data cleaning is done after data have been collected.
Data analysis takes place after the problem and data have been understood.
Collection follows deciding what problem needs to be solved and what data are needed.
This is correct: first understand the problem.

quiz.stem:
Q9.12. What does the 'Volume' characteristic of Big Data refer to?
(a) The speed at which data is generated
(b) The different forms data can take
(c) The sheer amount of data being collected
(d) The way data is processed
options: The speed at which data is generated
The different forms data can take
The sheer amount of data being collected
rationales: Speed of generation refers to the rate of data, not its volume.
Different forms refer to variety, not volume.
This is correct: volume is the sheer amount of data collected.
Processing method is not the meaning of volume.

quiz.stem:
Q9.13. What is an outlier in a dataset?
(a) The most frequent value
(b) The average of all values
(c) An unusual or extreme value that doesn't fit the pattern
(d) The middle value when all values are arranged in order
options: An unusual or extreme value that doesn't fit the pattern
The middle value when all values are arranged in order
rationales: The most frequent value is the mode, not an outlier.
The average is the mean, not an outlier.
This is correct: an outlier is an unusual or extreme value that does not fit the pattern.
The middle value is the median, not an outlier.

quiz.stem:
Q9.14. What does data encryption do?
(a) It converts data into a code to prevent unauthorized access.
(b) It makes data available to everyone online.
(c) It automatically deletes old data.
(d) It speeds up internet connection.
options: It converts data into a code to prevent unauthorized access.
It makes data available to everyone online.
rationales: This is correct: encryption codes data to prevent unauthorized access.
Encryption protects data; it does not make it available to everyone.
Encryption does not automatically delete old data.
Encryption does not speed up an internet connection.

For example, students' heights or the time taken to complete a test can be measured and may include values between whole numbers.

It can organise responses so that they are easier to analyse.
However, some students may not have access to the internet or a suitable device, and some may leave questions unanswered.
Questions must be clear and unbiased, and respondents' information should be protected.

written.text: Q9.7. Describe a situation where non-numeric data is essential. How would you collect, store, and analyse this type of data? Discuss the tools and techniques you would use to ensure the data is accurately interpreted.
modelAnswer: Non-numeric data are essential when a school wants to understand why students prefer particular clubs.
The school could collect written answers in a survey or ask students in interviews.
Responses could be stored in a spreadsheet with clear labels, or grouped into categories such as sport, creativity, and friendship.
The answers could be analysed by grouping similar ideas and counting how often they occur, while checking the original responses so their meanings are not misinterpreted.

written.text: Q9.8. Explain the concept of data visualization. How does it help in understanding complex data? Provide examples of different types of visualizations and their applications in real-life scenarios.
modelAnswer: Data visualization is the presentation of data as pictures, such as charts and graphs.
It makes complex information easier to understand and helps people see patterns and comparisons.
A line graph can show change over time, such as daily temperature or a business's sales each month.
A scatter plot displays paired values as points and can show a relationship, such as the relationship between study time and test scores.

written.text: Q9.10. Differentiate between nominal, ordinal, discrete, and continuous data. For each type, describe a suitable visualization technique and provide a specific example of how this technique can be used to represent that type of data effectively.
modelAnswer: Nominal data are categories with no implied order; for example, favourite fruit can be represented in a bar chart.
Ordinal data are categories with an order; for example, satisfaction levels can be shown in an ordered bar chart.
Discrete data have separate, countable values; for example, the number of books borrowed can be shown in a bar chart.
Continuous data are measured values that can take values within a range; for example, students' heights can be represented in a histogram.
